q: So many teachers who struggle with classroom management lack an understanding of purpose. In other words, they don’t fully understand the why of what they do.
The most immediate purpose of time-out is to separate the offending student from the rest of the class in order to protect their right to learn.
Time-out is a clear message, best learned by the students themselves, that anyone who interferes with learning is not welcome.
This is one reason why time-out should be at least 15 minutes before allowing the student to rejoin the class.
When you have a positive relationship with your students, when they trust you, admire you, and enjoy being in your class, then they’ll feel remorseful about misbehaving.
Time-out then becomes for your students not just a brief, mindless respite. But a behavior altering experience.

t: Why Intimidation Is A Terrible Classroom Management Strategy nagement-strategy/
q: Glaring, threatening, yelling, scolding, browbeating, pressuring, overbearing . . . few teachers would admit to using intimidation as a classroom management method, even to themselves.
Whenever fear enters the equation, to any degree, it’s hurtful to students.
Using intimidation is remarkably stressful—filling you with apprehension, weighing you down with often-unrecognized guilt, and causing you to be in a state of perpetual conflict with your students.
Most teachers who resort to hurtful methods like intimidation do so in lieu of following their classroom management plan—which amounts to going back on their word.
The use of intimidation doesn’t allow students to reflect on their misbehavior because they’re too busy boiling with anger at their teacher.
But there is a name for those who purposely use their position of power or authority to force others to do what they want: Bully.

t: Handling Difficult Students The First Week Of School school/
q: And when students feel labeled, they’re pulled inexorably in its direction—fulfilling the prophecy it foretells.
When a student with a difficult reputation walks in on the first day and is asked to sit closest to the teacher, she knows the score.
Your extra attention and frequent check-ins communicate loud and clear that you’ve got your eye on them, creating a distrustful relationship right from the get-go.
It’s common for teachers to speak to difficult students differently than others—without even realizing it.
By way of warning, it’s a common tactic to let difficult students know—in no uncertain terms—that you’re aware of their previous behavior problems. But this undermines your ability to build rapport.
Lasting change happens when we show students, when we prove to them, through our actions and our commitment to the same soaring standards as everyone else . . . That we believe in them.

t: Why Accountability Is Key To Building Rapport https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/08/04/why-accountability-is-key-to-building-rapport/
q: When students aren’t held accountable for misbehavior, they take advantage of it. They become brazen and disrespectful.
The truth is, accountability is the foundation upon which positive relationships with students are built.
A classroom management plan is a contract between you and your students that protects their right to learn and enjoy school in a peaceful environment.
A classroom management plan allows you to hold students accountable for misbehavior without causing friction or resentment.
Following your classroom management plan builds trust between you and your students because in a very concrete way it shows them that you can be counted on to do what you say you’re going to do.
The biggest surprise to teachers who make the unwavering commitment to hold students accountable is the reaction they get from their students.
